learningGoal.source: Explain how form, material and display can communicate authority, and compare works from different societies without assuming they mean the same thing.

evidence.question.source: Egypt's New Kingdom, around 1473–1458 BCE, and Moche societies on the north coast of present-day Peru, 400–700 CE. Look at each work's shape and materials first, then at its details.

read.sections.0.text.source:
Art can communicate authority, a recognised or claimed power to rule, through a ruler's image, an impressive setting, or objects worn on the body. Size, material, clothing and symbols can make status visible. Different societies connected art with political and religious life in different ways. A huge sculpture and a piece of jewellery offer two examples.

The Met's sphinx of Hatshepsut was made in ancient Egypt around 1473–1458 BCE. A lion's body supports the pharaoh's human head. The head wears a royal headcloth and a ceremonial false beard. Hatshepsut governed first as regent, someone who rules for another person, and then as senior co-ruler with Thutmose III. Her images followed established conventions, or usual ways, of showing a king. Yet some of her statues showed her as a woman.

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
Art can show authority. Authority is power to rule or lead. It can use a ruler's picture, a grand place or things people wear. Size, materials, clothes and symbols can show a person's rank. Each society linked art and power in its own way.

The sphinx of Hatshepsut is from ancient Egypt. It was made around 1473 to 1458 BCE. It has a lion's body and a human head. The head is Hatshepsut, a pharaoh, or ruler of Egypt. She wears a royal head cloth and a false beard for ceremonies. First, Hatshepsut ruled for someone else. Then she ruled alongside Thutmose III, as the senior ruler. Her statues often followed the usual conventions for showing kings. But some statues showed her as a woman.

read.sections.1.text.source:
This granite sphinx was one of at least six at Hatshepsut's mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri, a temple linked with her burial and memory. The strong animal body, royal features and great size connected the ruler with strength. A group of sphinxes joined sculpture to architecture and royal memory. The museum's sphinx was rebuilt from pieces found by excavation. Its preservation is another part of its history.

This was a setting in Egypt's New Kingdom, not one timeless style of Egyptian government. At Hatshepsut's temple, the central sanctuary, or holiest room, belonged to Amun-Re, a major god worshipped at nearby Karnak. Spaces for offerings also honoured Hatshepsut and her father, Thutmose I. So religious ceremonies and the royal family were connected in the way the building was arranged. A ruler could show links with earlier kings while honouring a god. Such a display could claim legitimacy, the accepted right to rule, but it does not prove that everyone accepted it. The sphinx belonged to this setting of worship and kingship. It was not a portrait standing on its own.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
This stone sphinx stood at her temple at Deir el-Bahri. It was one of at least six. The temple was linked with her burial and memory. The lion body and royal face linked her with strength. Its great size did too. The museum's sphinx was found broken. It was put back together from pieces dug up from the ground.

This was in Egypt's New Kingdom period. The temple's holiest room was for Amun-Re, an important god. Other rooms honoured Hatshepsut and her father. So worship and the royal family were joined in one building. The ruler showed links with past kings. She also honoured a god. This could support her legitimacy. That means people accept a ruler's right to rule. But it does not prove that everyone did. The sphinx was part of this temple. It was not a picture standing alone.

read.sections.2.text.source:
Across the Atlantic, Moche artists on the north coast of present-day Peru made an ear ornament with a winged runner around 400–700 CE. Gold surrounds a mosaic of turquoise, sodalite and shell. A mosaic is a picture made from small pieces. Moche communities built regional centres, farmed coastal deserts and used the Pacific Ocean's resources. They shared practices without forming one central state. They lived centuries before the Inca. "Peru" tells us where they lived in today's terms; it does not name their ancient nation.

The ornament's tube-shaped back fitted through a stretched earlobe and held up the decorated front. Objects like this marked out high-status people through their materials, craftsmanship and display on the body. Evidence shows that powerful women as well as men wore ear ornaments. This kind of adornment made the body a place for showing social position. That is different from meeting a huge sculpture in a temple.

The runner holds a small bag, but the exact meaning of the image is uncertain. Museo Larco, a museum in Peru, links the varied stones and shells in Moche ear ornaments with trade over long distances by powerful people. Skilled makers combined materials as well as designing images. This linked display on the body to a wider supply of valued resources.

Comparing the two works does not make Egyptian and Moche institutions the same. It shows how particular artists turned materials into different public signs of power, and why their historical settings matter.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Far away, in what is now Peru, Moche artists made an ear ornament. It is from about 400 to 700 CE. It shows a runner with wings. Gold goes around a mosaic. A mosaic is a picture made of small pieces. Here the pieces are blue and green stones and shell. Moche people built towns, farmed the desert and used the ocean. They shared ways of life. But they did not have one central government. They lived long before the Inca.

A tube on the back went through a stretched earlobe. Powerful people wore ornaments like this. Powerful women wore them too, not only men. This adornment showed a person's rank on their body. That is different from seeing a huge statue in a temple.

The runner holds a small bag. No one knows exactly what the picture means. A museum in Peru links the stones and shells with trade over long distances. Makers chose and joined these materials with skill.

The two works are very different. Both link art with power. But each belongs to its own place and time.

read.glossary.0.definition.source: A recognised or claimed power to rule or act.

read.glossary.0.example.source: The sphinx shows Hatshepsut's authority as a ruler.

read.glossary.1.definition.source: A usual, agreed way of showing or doing something.

read.glossary.1.example.source: The false beard was a convention for showing Egyptian kings.

read.glossary.2.definition.source: People's acceptance of a ruler's right to rule.

read.glossary.2.example.source: A temple could help a ruler claim legitimacy.

read.glossary.3.definition.source: A picture or pattern made from many small pieces.

read.glossary.3.example.source: The runner on the ear ornament is a mosaic of stones and shell.

read.glossary.4.definition.source: Something worn to decorate the body or show something about a person.

read.glossary.4.example.source: The gold ear ornament was an adornment for a powerful person.

write.prompt.source: Pick the sphinx or the ear ornament. Explain how one feature helps show authority or status. Give one fact from its history, and say which part of your answer is an interpretation. Two or three sentences are enough.

write.sentenceStarters.1.source: A fact from its history is ...

write.example.source: One feature of the sphinx is its lion's body with Hatshepsut's head and royal headcloth. A fact from its history is that it was one of at least six sphinxes at her temple, where a god and the royal family were honoured. My interpretation is that the strong lion body and the temple setting were meant to link her with strength and the gods. This does not prove that everyone accepted her rule.

speak.partnerTask.source: With a partner, explain one useful similarity and one important difference between the sphinx and the ear ornament.

speak.independentTask.source: Say or type a short comparison of the two works: one similarity and one difference.

reflect.prompts.0.text.source: Before explaining an artwork's message, one thing I would want to know about the people who first saw it is ...

reflect.completionMessage.source: You finished Lesson 4. You saw how a stone sphinx and a gold ear ornament showed power in two different societies.

visual.alt.source: A reddish speckled granite sphinx lies on a stone base, its front paws stretched forward. It has a lion's body and a calm human face wearing a striped royal headcloth and a long false beard.

visual.caption.source: Sphinx of Hatshepsut, about 1473–1458 BCE. Maker not recorded. Granite and paint. Ancient Egypt, New Kingdom. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

secondVisual.alt.source: A round ear ornament ringed by large gold beads. Inside a thin gold frame, a mosaic of turquoise, blue stone and shell shows a running figure with wings and a bird's beak, wearing an orange kilt and holding a small bag.

secondVisual.caption.source: Ear ornament with winged runner, 400–700 CE. Moche artists. Gold, turquoise, sodalite and shell. North coast of present-day Peru. One of a pair. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: The sphinx stood at a mortuary temple, linked with Hatshepsut's burial and memory, and the temple honoured the god Amun-Re. Teach these as historical beliefs and practices; no learner is asked to share their own beliefs. The ear ornament was worn through a stretched earlobe. Treat this as historical evidence of status, not something to try; don't invite comments on anyone's body or appearance.

educatorNotes.0.source: Grandeur doesn't prove that everyone supported a ruler. Don't confuse the Moche with the later Inca or call them one central empire, and explain that the sphinx was rebuilt from excavated pieces.

educatorNotes.1.source: Answer points for Write: accept a supported link between royal form, size, setting, valuable material, skilled making or display on the body and authority or status. Don't identify the Moche wearer, insist on one meaning for the runner, or mark learners on agreeing with an expert.

educatorNotes.2.source: The temple's central sanctuary for Amun-Re and the offering spaces for Hatshepsut and Thutmose I come from Dieter Arnold's essay on The Met's model of the temple (2023); its broad judgements comparing political societies aren't used. The model is context, not a lesson image.

educatorNotes.3.source: How ear ornaments were worn, and evidence of powerful women wearing them, come from Ji Mary Seo's article for The Met (2018). Moche long-distance trade comes from Museo Larco's online exhibition of Mochica gold ear ornaments; it is general context, and The Met's ornament isn't one of Larco's objects.

educatorNotes.4.source: Use The Met's current date for the ear ornament (400–700 CE), not older publications' dates. The photograph shows one ornament of a pair: don't caption it as two objects or use the companion's accession number. The sphinx's number is 31.3.166; don't confuse it with other Hatshepsut sphinxes.
